questions.prompt: Why is Milo's repeated sofa scratching useful evidence rather than proof of spite?

options.text: Its repeated site and vertical stretch reveal a location, surface, and orientation preference.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Scratching is normal marking behaviour, and the chosen site helps the household design an alternative that can genuinely compete.

options.text: Repeating the act means she understands the rule and is testing whether punishment will follow.
options.feedback: Repetition does not establish a spiteful intention. Punishment fails to meet the scratching need and can add stress without creating the intended association.

options.text: The damage matters, but the place and body position do not influence the response.
options.feedback: Those details are central. An outlet that fails to match the observed surface, orientation, and location may exist without being useful to Milo.

questions.prompt: Which response best supports a cat's predatory-play need?

options.text: Use hands as prey so the cat receives realistic close-range feedback.
options.feedback: Hands and feet should stay out of the prey role. Rehearsing attacks on people makes the outlet less safe and less sustainable.

options.text: Use wand-led stalk, chase, and capture opportunities, plus safe foraging and toy rotation.
options.feedback: This is the best answer because it provides a species-typical sequence and safe endpoint rather than trying to suppress the underlying drive.

options.text: Offer more food whenever pouncing begins because hunting is always a sign of hunger.
options.feedback: Predatory motivation persists even in a well-fed cat. Food alone does not replace the behavioural sequence the cat is trying to perform.

questions.prompt: What is the correct first interpretation of a new raw bald patch caused by repeated licking?

options.text: It is probably boredom, so add play before considering another cause.
options.feedback: Enrichment may matter later, but a new raw patch first requires a veterinarian to rule out physical and medical causes.

options.text: It is an observation to report for veterinary rule-out before labelling the behaviour stress-related.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Location and extent are useful owner observations, while determining pain, itch, or another cause remains clinical work.

options.text: It confirms a local pain source because localised licking has only one possible cause.
options.feedback: A localised pattern can inform the report but cannot confirm a diagnosis. The source supports medical-first elimination, not owner diagnosis.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter's 'needs, not naughtiness' synthesis require?

options.text: Apply enrichment to every unwanted behaviour because all problems are unmet needs.
options.feedback: The synthesis includes a medical-first branch. Treating every problem as enrichment would be especially unsafe for overgrooming or an urgent elimination pattern.

options.text: Identify whether the case needs environmental redirect, play redirect, medical rule-out, or urgent escalation before responding.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The shared question organises triage but preserves the distinct response each observed behaviour requires.

options.text: Avoid intervention entirely because species-typical behaviour should never be redirected.
options.feedback: Normal needs can be given safer, acceptable outlets. Understanding function does not require accepting harm to the cat, people, or home.

questions.prompt: Milo pounces on feet moving under a blanket, then crouches toward a wand toy with forward attention and no distance-increasing signals. What is the best response?

options.text: Redirect the sequence to the wand toy and allow a safe capture away from hands and feet.
options.feedback: This is the best response because the combined cues support predatory play and the alternative preserves the sequence without rehearsing people as prey.

options.text: Continue moving feet because play between a cat and household members is harmless if nobody is injured yet.
options.feedback: This keeps feet in the prey role and strengthens the pattern the household is trying to redirect, even if the immediate interaction seems playful.

options.text: Spray Milo because pouncing is deliberate aggression and must have an immediate consequence.
options.feedback: The described signals fit a predatory-play reading more strongly than deliberate aggression. Punishment does not supply a safe outlet and may add stress.

questions.prompt: A household cannot afford a commercial cat tree, and Milo scratches a vertical doorframe. Which plan best applies the evidence?

options.text: Use a stable low-cost vertical material that matches the surface near the doorframe, while recognising the specific DIY form as a course application.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The direct principle is matching orientation, surface, stability, and location; an inexpensive implementation can still satisfy it.

options.text: Consider declawing because the one-time cost may be lower than replacing furniture and posts.
options.feedback: Cost does not make an invasive amputation-equivalent procedure a proportionate first response to normal scratching behaviour.

options.text: Buy the cheapest horizontal pad and put it in another room because any scratching object should work.
options.feedback: Price alone is not the issue. A horizontal, distant outlet ignores the vertical and location preferences revealed by the doorframe.

questions.prompt: In one week Milo scratches furniture, pounces on feet, and develops a raw licked patch. Why is 'more toys for everything' an incomplete plan?

options.text: Toys are never useful for cats once scratching and grooming occur together.
options.feedback: Toy-led play may be useful for the pouncing. The problem is treating one potentially helpful tool as the answer to every different mechanism.

options.text: Each behaviour needs separate triage, and the raw patch cannot safely wait behind a general enrichment experiment.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis. It matches the scratching environment, redirects play, and preserves medical-first reasoning for visible skin change.

options.text: Three behaviours at once prove that Milo has a single stress disorder requiring medication.
options.feedback: The household cannot diagnose a single cause from co-occurrence, and medication remains veterinarian-led after appropriate rule-out.
